title: ～ちゃいけない / ～じゃいけない — the casual “you must not ～”
summary: The spoken, contracted form of ～てはいけない. The て of the te-form shrinks to ちゃ (and で to じゃ), giving a casual “you must not ～ / it’s not allowed.” Used with friends and in relaxed situations.

patterns.form: Vて［て］＋ ちゃいけない
patterns.gloss: te-form ending in て → ちゃ (e.g. 食べて → 食べちゃいけない)

patterns.form: Vて［で］＋ じゃいけない
patterns.gloss: te-form ending in で → じゃ (e.g. 飲んで → 飲んじゃいけない)

body.p: It is ～てはいけない with ては squeezed together in speech. 食べては → 食べちゃ, 見ては → 見ちゃ. Verbs whose te-form ends in で (飲んで, 読んで, 遊んで) become じゃ: 飲んで → 飲んじゃ.
Because it is casual, keep it for friends, family and people close to you. On signs, in writing, or when speaking politely, use the full ～てはいけません or ～ないでください instead.
You can swap the final いけない for だめ with no change in meaning, just an even more casual feel: 触っちゃだめ (“don’t touch it”). It talks about what is forbidden now or from now on, not a past action.

examples.ja: ここで写真（しゃしん）を撮（と）っちゃいけないよ。
examples.romaji: Koko de shashin o totcha ikenai yo.
examples.tr: You must not take photos here.
examples.note: 撮って → 撮っちゃ. The final よ is a soft reminder.

examples.ja: ここでご飯（はん）を食（た）べちゃいけないよ。
examples.romaji: Koko de gohan o tabecha ikenai yo.
examples.note: 食べて → 食べちゃ (te-form ends in て).

examples.ja: その水（みず）を飲（の）んじゃいけないよ。
examples.romaji: Sono mizu o nonja ikenai yo.
examples.note: 飲んで ends in で, so it becomes 飲んじゃ, not 飲んちゃ.

pitfalls: Match the sound: te-forms ending in て take ちゃ, those ending in で take じゃ. It is 飲んじゃ, not 飲んちゃ.
It is casual. On official signs or when being polite, use ～てはいけません instead.
